newsitem.title: USA: Congress seeks to overhaul loan disclosure laws.
newsitem.headline: Congress seeks to overhaul loan disclosure laws.

text.p: Congress sees a need to overhaul two U.S. laws requiring clearer disclosure on consumer loans but is unlikely to approve a reform bill until next year, legislators said Tuesday.
Enacted in the 1970s, the Truth in Lending Act and the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Acts were intended to deter deceptive sales practices and to help consumers comparison shop for loans.
But the mortgage market has changed substantially over the past 20 years and surveys now indicate many consumers are bewildered by the often confusing loan process.
"While no one finds fault with these objectives, in reality, these statutes are hurting consumers," Sen. Lauch Faircloth, a North Carolina Republican, said at a hearing to discuss reforming the laws.

Federal regulators are meeting with consumer and industry groups to try to come up with a reform proposal supported by all, said Faircloth, chairman of the Senate Banking Committee's financial institutions subcommittee. All agree that the laws should be changed, but they have yet to reach a consensus about what changes should be made.
"I look forward to seeing what the parties have agreed upon next year so that we can pass legislation to give consumers information and choices when buying a home," Faircloth said.

Regulators at the hearing said one problem was the timing of disclosures related to the cost of a loan. Currently, consumer borrowers cannot receive mandated disclosures about loan costs until after they have paid a non-refundable application fee.

Another controversial aspect of the laws, disclosure of fees paid to mortgage brokers, will be addressed in a proposed rule to be issued later this summer by the Department of Housing and Urban Development, assistant HUD Secretary Nicholas Retsinas said.

Consumers who use a mortgage broker to secure a loan may not realise that the broker can be paid a fee by the mortgage lender. Consumer groups charge that one type of undisclosed fee, called a "yield spread premium," is paid by lenders to brokers for persuading a borrower to pay a higher rate of interest.
In most states, the broker is under no legal obligation to the borrower to find the best loan deal, although consumers often believe such an obligation exists.

Dozens of lawsuits are pending alleging that the payment of yield spread premiums violates the Real Estate Settlement law. Some in the mortgage industry have asked Congress to impose a moratorium on the lawsuits until the law is reformed, but few legislators voiced support for such a move.
